_comment: THE CAMPAIGN'S MACHINE REGISTRY -- one entry per participant, frozen 2026-08-05.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS.  --machine k was passed by hand on every launch, and a
typo there is the worst failure the harness has: two machines silently claim
the same rows and leave a hole somewhere else, which shows up at merge time
as 'rows MISSING' -- indistinguishable from a machine that never reported.
Detection removes the hand-typed index.
DETECTION FAILS LOUDLY, NEVER GUESSES.  An unrecognised host is an error, not
a default, for exactly the reason above.  To bring a new host online, run
python run_ensemble.py --register <index>
which appends this host's fingerprint to the matching entry.
WHY NOT HOSTNAME ALONE.  platform.node() on the Macs returns the DHCP name
'Mac.san.rr.com', and the v2 pool shows TWO PHYSICALLY DIFFERENT Macs (16-core
and 8-core) reporting that same string.  Hostname is matched only where it is
actually distinctive; the Macs are pinned on hw.model + core count as well.
WEIGHTS ARE FROZEN.  Changing a weight re-partitions the design, so rows
already computed change owner and get recomputed by somebody else.  Do not
edit `weight` mid-campaign; add capacity with --subtask instead.
SPEED PROVENANCE -- measured unless stated:
0 MacBook Pro   1.000  reference. 3780 s/row mean at the rev-6 grid,
1 Matrix-PC     0.400  DECLARED. Its manifest never arrived; the v2 pool
gives 2.7x-15x slower depending on how it is read.
2 Workstation   0.500  DECLARED by the author 2026-08-05. Never contributed
a row. Replace with a measurement when it has.
3 Hoffman2      0.214  measured: job 14223957 ran the reference row in
26059.6 s against the Mac's 5580.6 s, observables
matching to printed precision (plan S12(r)).

machines.name: Matrix-PC
_slots_note: slots RAISED 4 -> 20 on 2026-08-07; `weight` deliberately LEFT AT 1.6.
The two are decoupled at runtime: run_ensemble takes workers from
`slots` (line ~1013) but the row->machine map from the top-level
`weights` STRING (line ~1044), so this change cannot re-partition the
design and no completed row changes owner.  weights_map_sha is
unchanged by construction; only weights_sha (the file hash) moves.
WHY 20 AND NOT 40.  The host is 2x Xeon Gold 6230 = 40 physical / 80
logical cores.  Windows splits >64 logical CPUs into two processor
GROUPS of 40 logical each (= one socket), and a process is confined to
the group it was created in -- measured 2026-08-07: all solver.exe sat
on group 0 while socket 1 idled at 0%.  So only 20 PHYSICAL cores are
reachable.  20 workers = one per physical core.  Going higher would
oversubscribe onto HT siblings and LENGTHEN every row, which is exactly
wrong here: this machine's problem is a per-row deadline, not throughput.
Using socket 1 needs group-aware affinity, or two --of-subtasks
processes pinned one per group.  Not attempted.
TIMEOUT.  The global 3600 s was calibrated from machine 0's MEASURED
distribution (see timeout_note) -- an M3 Max.  This host is ~13x slower
at equal dose (archived T2 campaign, both machines at median 0.1 dpa:
6990 s here vs 528 s on the Mac).  T2 needed 6990 s for 0.1 dpa; T3
asks for 1.0 dpa in 3600 s, roughly half the time this box needed for a
tenth of the dose.  Result: 52 of 52 rows starved at a median 0.0027
dpa and reached NO rung of the dose ladder.  50400 s (14 h) is an
overnight budget for this host only; other machines have no override
and keep the global value.

machines.name: Nasr Workstation
_slots_note: slots LOWERED 14 -> 12 on 2026-08-08; `weight` deliberately LEFT AT 7.0,
for the same reason entry 1 leaves its weight alone: run_ensemble takes
workers from `slots` but the row->machine map from the top-level
`weights` STRING, so this cannot re-partition the design and no
completed row changes owner.  weights_map_sha is unchanged; only
weights_sha (the file hash) moves.
WHY 12.  Win32_Processor reports 1 x Xeon Silver 4116: 12 PHYSICAL
cores, 24 logical.  14 workers therefore ran two of the twelve cores
with a pair of solver.exe on HT siblings, so those two rows ran slow
for no extra throughput.  This machine's problem is a per-row DEADLINE,
not throughput -- a starved row is admissible and still pools, it just
never reaches the high rungs where the screening happens -- so a slow
row is a wasted row.  12 workers = one per physical core.
_timeout_note: PER-MACHINE BUDGET, 4.5 h, from this host's own 112 rows of T3 rev 6.
THE OVERRIDE ONLY STARTED WORKING ON 2026-08-08.  Entries 1 and 3 have
carried timeout_s since 2026-08-07, but nothing read it: the notebook
passes the top-level reg['timeout_s'] to --timeout-s for everyone.  It
is now resolved --timeout-s > this key > top-level > 3600.
MEASURED.  Of 112 rows at a 12000 s budget and 14 workers, 104 were cut
(93 %) at a median 0.059 dpa, and only 8 reached 1.0 dpa.  The eight
that finished are the tell: their walls are 8569, 10909, 11626, 11659,
11665, 11670, 11878, 11924 s -- six of the eight inside the last 300 s
before the cap.  That is a censored distribution whose bulk sits just
ABOVE 12000 s, so the cap was cutting through the densest part of it and
a modest raise converts a disproportionate number of rows.
RAISED 16200 -> 28800 s (8 h) on 2026-08-08, on MEASUREMENT.
WHAT 16200 s ACTUALLY DELIVERED: 24 rows ran under it (all N5, because
rows are taken in row_id order and 472..565 are contiguous N5).  FIVE
reached 1.0 dpa = 21 %.  Full-dose walls 12233, 13132, 13343, 13381,
13447 s; the other 19 were cut at ~16264 s holding 0.06-0.49 dpa.
ALL FIVE needed more than the OLD 12000 s cap, so those same 24 rows
would have returned ZERO full-dose rows under the previous budget.
BEWARE THE FIRST BATCH.  Batch 1 alone was 4/12 = 33 % and briefly
looked like a win over the 19 % the model predicted; batch 2 was 1/12.
Pooled, 5/24 = 21 %, i.e. the model was right and the 33 % was small-
sample noise.  One batch of 12 is not a rate -- do not re-tune off one.
Anchored on 21 %, this host is ~3.56x slower than machine 3.
WHY RAISE AT ALL.  The 21 % above describes N5.  What REMAINS is 80 I1
+ 24 N5, and I1 is the condition this host has never run.  Everywhere
else it is the best-behaved one -- 17/17 full dose on machine 1, 52/52
on machine 3, and cheaper than N5 on the same host (p50 19271 vs 34084
s on machine 1).  Scaled by 3.56x, this host's I1 median lands near
22 ks: JUST ABOVE the 16200 cap, the worst place for a cutoff, since
nearly the whole cost of a row is paid and then the row is lost at the
last step.  Projected yield of the remaining 104 rows:
28800 s was the value authorised and is set here.  NOTE the knee is
arguably 36000 s: it finishes I1 outright for +11 rows and +18 h, and
past that only a slow N5 sub-population is left, which no realistic
budget recovers (54000 s buys 1.6 rows for 43 h).
STILL TO VERIFY: the I1 column is SCALED from machine 3, not measured
here.  The first I1 rows to land are the test; if their walls run past
~28 ks then 28800 s is cutting into I1 and 36000 s is the right value.
NOT A LEVER: intra-row OpenMP.  solver.exe does link VCOMP140.DLL and
the active_window kernels are OpenMP loops, but they are guarded by
if(x_hi_i_win + x_hi_v_win > 500) and solver.cpp clamps x_hi_i below
N_EQ-1.  The frozen bin_moment grid has N_EQ = 135, so the parallel
region can never open and --omp-threads is a no-op HERE.  It would
matter only to a `discrete` campaign, where the SIA states number I.

machines.name: MacBook Air
_timeout_note: PER-MACHINE BUDGET, 2 h.  `weight` is deliberately LEFT AT 6.8 -- only
the row budget is local, so this cannot re-partition the design and no
completed row changes owner.
MEASURED, not declared, from this host's own first 89 rows (T3 rev 6,
the frozen grid, 8-way concurrency).  Wall distribution: p25 4580 s,
p50 6012 s, p75 12721 s, p90 16087 s -- against the global 3600 s that
was calibrated from machine 0's M3 Max.  Fraction of the 71 full-dose
rows that would still have reached 1.0 dpa under a row budget X:
7200 s is the knee: 9000 s costs 25 % more per row for 6 more points.
At 3600 s this host would starve ~4 of every 5 rows it can finish, and
a starved row is still admissible and still lands in the pool -- it
just never reaches the high rungs where the screening happens.
Re-measure once a batch has run under THIS budget; the numbers above
come from rows that ran under the old per-segment 12000 s setting.
machines._note: Replaces Hoffman2, withdrawn 2026-08-05 after every row failed on its COMPUTE nodes at the production grid (TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable, 5-8 s per row). CAUSE NARROWED, NOT FOUND -- and NOT memory: a follow-up job on node n1032 ran the SAME row (59) at the SAME grid (I=30000/V=5000) to rc=0 with peak RSS 161 MB, ulimit -v unlimited and 16 G granted. What differs is the CALL PATH: that row succeeded through a direct RE.evaluate(), while the array job goes through run_ensemble's multiprocessing pool (--workers 4). The same pool path also worked on a compute node at I=300/V=480, so it is the combination of the pool and the production grid. Linux uses fork() where macOS uses spawn, and cpp_bridge drains solver stdout on threads -- fork+threads is the obvious suspect and is UNVERIFIED. *** THIS MAY ALSO AFFECT ANY LINUX PARTICIPANT, including machine 2. Before trusting a Linux machine's rows, run it with --limit 2 and confirm the rows take ~1 h, not seconds. hoffman2_array.sh and hoffman2_setup.sh are retained. With no registry entry, running on Hoffman2 fails detection loudly. MacBook Air speed 0.85 is DECLARED and deliberately below its burst figure: the Air is fanless and this is a 30+ h all-core load. Measure it from the first manifest; do NOT edit the weight mid-campaign -- that repartitions the design.

grid_note: FROZEN by the author 2026-08-06 for a 24-48 h campaign. Every participant reads THIS block -- the notebook builds its command line from it, so the grid is never retyped per machine. Measured 2026-08-06 at 10-way concurrency on the M3 Max, same design row (21), against the I=30000/V=5000 /b25/i_mobile=50 base at 4171 s: I=10000 alone is 1838 s (2.3x) and moves the FOUR SCREENED observables by <=6% (d_111 +2%, N_111 +4%, mean_n_v +2%); it truncates <100>, which is already withheld by BIN_MOMENT_BLOCKED. V stays 5000: V=2000 collapses mean_n_v 2682->816 (-70%) and V=1000 to 362, and N_voids/d_cavity_nm are two of the four screened observables. dose stays 1.0: halving it saves only 17% (4171->3467 s), and 0-7% at the smaller grids -- 0.5->1.0 dpa is one time doubling out of ~8 decades of a stiff integration -- while a linear 0.1-0.5 dpa extrapolation mispredicts the run's OWN 1.0 dpa value by 30-85%, systematically in sign. i_mobile 50->40 and bins 25->20 are the author's call. i_mobile is PHYSICS, not a numerical knob: at 30 it moved N_100 +109%, N_111 -18%, d_111 -9%, so results here are NOT comparable with anything run at i_mobile=50. i_discrete follows i_mobile (must be >= it).
timeout_note: ROW-LEVEL budget, 1 h. Enforced since 2026-08-06 in simulation.py: it used to be handed to EVERY segment unchanged, so a row could run n_segments x the limit -- rows of 16108-20503 s completed under a 12000 s setting and the cap never bit. Now the budget is set once per row and each segment gets only what remains; the last one is cut gracefully so the partial trajectory and its dose-ladder rungs survive. Verified: a 300 s budget produced a 361 s row (61 s graceful-finalize allowance), starved=True, admissible=True, rc=0. Chosen from the MEASURED bimodal distribution on machine 0: ~30 % of rows finish in ~1700 s, the rest exceed 5000 s and were blocking 10 of 14 workers indefinitely. At a 3600 s cap the mean row is ~0.3*1700+0.7*3600 = 3030 s, giving ~16.6 rows/h on 14 slots -> ~29 h for 1008 rows on machine 0 ALONE, and less with the others. A 2400 s cap would reach ~21 h but cuts more rows at a lower dose; 3600 s keeps more of them at full dose inside the window.
